sections.body:
A currency is the money that a state, or a union of states, issues and backs. The euro is issued for the countries of the euro area and is backed by the European Central Bank. The naira is issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria. What makes money the currency of a country is not the paper or the metal; it is the decision of a public authority to stand behind it, and the habit of using it. A currency is two things at once: a promise and a habit.

Legal tender is the money the law accepts as the final payment of a debt. When a shop says it takes legal tender, it means that no court will let the buyer refuse the payment because the note is not his, or because he prefers another form of payment. The protection runs both ways: the law also requires the money to be the right money, and it lets the shop refuse a note that is badly damaged or counterfeit.

Every currency also carries a name for machines. The **ISO 4217 code** is a set of three letters that names the currency in the standard ISO 4217: USD, EUR, JPY, NGN. A bank, a customs office and an accounting system work with the code, not with the word dollar. Beside the code sits the symbol: the mark that people write and print on a price — $, €, ¥, ₹. The code and the symbol are the labels of the currency; the currency itself is the promise behind them.

Two things must hold for a currency to work. The state must keep its side of the promise: the money must be redeemable, and the prices must not run away from it. The people must keep theirs: the note must be accepted by the next shop, the next taxi driver and the next employer. The first is law and policy. The second is habit. A currency fails when either side stops.
examples: The euro is issued by the European Central Bank and is legal tender across the euro area.
Write USD on the invoice, not the word dollar, so the system reads it.
A court will accept legal tender as the final payment of a debt.
A currency is a promise and a habit: one from the state, one from the people.
sections.heading: What a currency is, in law and in practice

terms.example: The landlord must take legal tender for the rent, even when he prefers a transfer.
terms.gloss: The money the law accepts as the final payment of a debt, so that no one can refuse it as the wrong money.

terms.example: Write USD on the invoice, not the word dollar, so the system reads it.
terms.gloss: The three-letter code that names a currency in the standard ISO 4217, used by banks, customs offices and computer systems.

sections.body:
One name can serve many countries. The dollar is used in the United States, in Canada, in Australia and in a long list of other states. The euro serves the countries of the euro area. Most of these names are old: a franc, a dinar, a peso, a pound, a rupee, a shilling, an escudo, a kwanza, a ringgit, a taka, a baht and a yen are words that travelled with trade, with empires and with borders. A name carries a history, never a value. The dollar of one country is not the dollar of another, and the yen of Japan is not the yuan of China.

The name does not tell you who issues the money. That is the job of a **currency union**: an arrangement in which several states use one currency and one authority issues it and speaks for the whole group. The euro area is the largest such union, and the two CFA franc unions, one in West Africa and one in Central Africa, are smaller ones of the same kind. The **currency board** is a different arrangement: the country keeps its own money and its own name, but a foreign currency acts as the reserve that backs it, and the two are kept close together, so the local money cannot drift far from the other one. In a union, one issuer speaks for many countries. Under a board, the money keeps its own name and answers to another one.

Three different things carry the name of a currency, and they are not the same thing. The **name** is the word people say: dollar, euro, yen, rupiah, naira. The **code** is the three letters of the standard ISO 4217 that name it in a system: USD, EUR, JPY, IDR, NGN. The **symbol** is the mark that is written on the price. One currency can have many symbols, because every country that uses the name prints its own mark on its own notes. A symbol says even less than a name: the dollar sign appears on Canadian notes and on American notes alike, and those notes are different currencies.

One currency can serve many countries, and one country can use the money of another. When a country gives up its own currency and uses the currency of another country as its own money, the country is said to be **dollarized**. A dollarized country issues no notes of its own; it uses the notes of the country whose money it adopted, and that country keeps the right to issue there. The reason is practical. A stable money that the rest of the world already accepts is easier to trade with, and a small state cannot afford to run a central bank and defend a currency of its own.

The count of 195 is the count of the United Nations: the 193 member states, and the two observer states, the Holy See and the State of Palestine. Two states that are not in that count are not in the tables of this article either: Taiwan, whose money is the New Taiwan dollar, and Kosovo, whose money is the euro.
examples: The dollar is one name and many currencies, so always write the code.
The euro area is a currency union: one issuer, many countries.
Under a currency board the local money keeps its own name and stays close to another currency.
A dollarized country uses the notes of another country and issues none of its own.
sections.heading: One name, many countries: the families of currency

terms.example: The euro area is a currency union, so one central bank issues the notes for every member country.
terms.gloss: An arrangement in which several states use one currency and a single authority issues it for all of them.

terms.example: The country is dollarized: the shops take dollars and nobody issues local notes.
terms.gloss: The use, by a country, of the currency of another country as its own money, with no domestic currency issued.

terms.example: The contract says EUR; that is the ISO code, whatever the invoice calls it in words.
terms.gloss: The three-letter code that names a currency in the standard ISO 4217, used by banks, customs offices and computer systems.

sections.body:
Africa holds the largest number of distinct currencies of any continent: fifty-four countries, and forty-two different currencies, because the eight members of the West African CFA franc and the six members of the Central African CFA franc share one money each.

The row that carries the most weight in daily life is the franc of the CFA zones. The **CFA franc** is not a French franc in any sense that matters to the person who is paid in it: it is the currency of a currency union, issued by a common central bank, and its two codes — XOF in the west and XAF in the centre — exist because the two unions were set up separately and never merged. The franc is divided into 100 centimes, and the coins in circulation are 5, 10, 25, 50 and 100 francs.

The row that surprises visitors is the one for Ethiopia: the birr, still one of the largest currencies in Africa by unit of account, and a country that has been inside a crawling peg to the dollar since 2023. The namibian dollar, the somali shilling, the ghanaian cedi with its cedi sign that looks like a letter C with a bar through it — each of them is a money with its own history, and the history is told in the other sections of this article.
examples: The row of Ghana reads cedi, GHS, ₵, and the smallest unit of it is the pesewa.
Two currencies of this table have the same name and two different codes: XOF in the west and XAF in the centre.
sections.heading: The currencies of Africa

sections.body:
Asia carries the widest spread of money in the world: forty-eight countries, and forty-seven different currencies, because the State of Palestine uses the shekel of Israel and Timor-Leste uses the dollar of the United States.

Two families dominate the region and they pull in opposite directions. The **rupee** is the family of South Asia — India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal, the Maldives — and the name comes from the silver coin that the empire of India stamped with a wheel. The **rupiah** is the family of South-East Asia: Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, where it is called the ringgit, a word that means "brass".

The currencies that are not divided are the ones to watch. The yen of Japan, the won of Korea and the riel of Cambodia are used as whole units, and a price that ends in a round number is normal there. The dinar of the Gulf states goes the other way: it is divided into a thousand fils, and it is one of the heaviest coins in the world for its size, because the currency of a small oil state has to travel well.
examples: The row of Japan reads yen, JPY, ¥, and the yen is not divided at all.
The row of Palestine reads the shekel of Israel, and the code of that shekel is ILS.
sections.heading: The currencies of Asia

sections.body:
Europe is the one continent where most countries do not have a currency of their own: twenty-four of the forty-four countries here use the euro, and several others hold their money in a currency that belongs to somebody else. The euro is the largest currency area in the world by the number of people who use it, and the smallest by the number of currencies it has replaced.

The countries that kept their own money are mostly in the east and the north. Their currencies are older than the euro and they carry their history in the name: the **leu** of Romania and Moldova, the **lev** of Bulgaria, the **złoty** of Poland, the **koruna** of Czechia, the **forint** of Hungary, the **krona** of Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Iceland, the **pound sterling** of the United Kingdom. One of the small coins of the region is met nowhere else: the Moldovan **ban**, a hundredth of a leu, whose name comes from the small leather coins used in the region under the Ottoman rule. The **stotinka** of Bulgaria, a hundredth of a lev, and the **fening** of Bosnia, a hundredth of the convertible mark, are the small coins of the Balkans.

The currency of the far north stands apart. The **króna** of Iceland is one of the oldest currencies still in use, and it is not divided: there is no coin smaller than one króna in circulation.
examples: The row of Poland reads złoty, PLN, zł, and the smallest unit of it is the grosz.
Twenty-four rows of this table carry the same code, EUR, and the same sign, the euro.
sections.heading: The currencies of Europe

sections.body:
Twenty-three countries, and seventeen currencies between them, because six small states share one money: the **Eastern Caribbean dollar** is the currency of Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Its code is XCD and its coins are the same size as the coins of the United States, because the two currencies have been tied to each other since 1976.

Three countries of this region use the dollar of the United States as their own currency: El Salvador, Ecuador and Panama. Panama also has its own money, the **balboa**, which is issued in the same coins and the same notes as the dollar, and which exists so that the country can print a currency of its own without an exchange rate of its own.

The Caribbean carries the small coins of the world. The **centavo** of the Dominican Republic, the Jamaican dollar and the Cuban peso all divide into a hundred. The colón of Costa Rica keeps the sign of the peso with two strokes through it, ₡, and it is a sign that only one country in the world uses.
examples: The row of Panama reads balboa, PAB, B/., and the smallest unit of it is the centésimo.
Six rows of this table carry the code XCD, the Eastern Caribbean dollar.
sections.heading: The currencies of North America and the Caribbean

sections.body:
Twelve countries, and eleven currencies of their own: Ecuador uses the dollar of the United States, and Bolivia has replaced its peso with the **boliviano**, a currency that takes its name from the country and not from the coin.

The continent is the home of the paper money with the most colour in the world. The Argentine peso, the Brazilian real and the Colombian peso are printed in the colours of the flags of their countries, and the real — the word means "royal" — was named for the portrait of the king that the first notes carried.

Two of these currencies are not divided at all. The **Chilean peso** has no coin smaller than one peso, and the **guaraní** of Paraguay has no coin in circulation either: both countries write prices in whole units and round them. The **sol** of Peru is the odd one out in the other direction: it was replaced in 1991 to stop the country counting in a currency that had lost most of its value, and its name is the word for the sun that the old coins of the Inca carried.
examples: The row of Brazil reads real, BRL, R$, and the smallest unit of it is the centavo.
The row of Ecuador carries the dollar of the United States, and the code of that dollar is USD.
sections.heading: The currencies of South America

sections.body:
Fourteen countries, and nine currencies. Seven of them use a money that belongs to somebody else: Australia, Nauru, Tuvalu and Kiribati use the Australian dollar, and the Marshall Islands, Micronesia and Palau use the dollar of the United States.

The currencies of the islands are small in number and light in weight. The **kina** of Papua New Guinea is named after the shell that the people of the coast used as money before the country had a currency of its own, and its smallest coin is the **toea**, a hundredth of a kina. The **tālā** of Samoa is one of the few currencies in the world whose notes and coins carry the picture of a person who is alive: the head of the state.

The **paʻanga** of Tonga is divided, and the **seniti**, a hundredth of a paʻanga, is its smallest coin. Tonga is also one of the few countries in the world whose coins do not carry a leading zero: the value on the coin is written as it is, without the zero of the cents.
examples: The row of Tonga reads paʻanga, TOP, T$, and the smallest unit of it is the seniti.
Four rows of this table carry the Australian dollar, and three more carry the dollar of the United States.
sections.heading: The currencies of Oceania

sections.body:
A piece of money in your hand carries at least two facts: what it is worth, and who stands behind it. The **denomination** is the value printed on it — 5, 20, 500, 1 000 — and it is the first thing anyone reads. Under the value there is usually the mark of the issuer, so that the holder can tell at a glance which country backs the piece. Some notes carry a portrait, a building or a plant, and some carry a sentence that states the promise in words. A coin carries the same two facts in a smaller space: the number of the value, and the mark of the country that issues it.

Above the value there is a smaller unit. The **minor unit** is the part of a currency that people rarely see: the cent of the dollar, the cent of the euro, the penny of the pound, the fils of the dinar. A price is normally written in the major unit — 12.50 — but the money in circulation is made of both. That is why a note of 20 and a purse full of coins of 50 cents feel like different amounts of money, even when the two add up to the same number.

Some currencies are not divided at all. The yen and the won are used without a smaller unit in ordinary shops, and in much of Cambodia the riel is the same: the price is a whole number, and the cashier cannot give change below one unit. When a country works this way, the prices are written as whole numbers, and the cashier rounds the total to the unit that can be paid. Other countries have small units that nobody carries. A shop that takes cash asks whether to round the total to the nearest convenient note, and the answer is often yes. The difference stays in the shop.

Not all money is in your pocket. The same purchase can be made with a banknote, with coins, or by a number in a phone. A **cash economy** is a country where most payments are still made in cash, and in such a country the note and the coin are not a leftover from an older age; they are the normal way to pay. The reasons are practical: a small shop may have no machine, the network may not reach it, the customer may not carry a card, and in many places the law says that a shop may not refuse cash. In a country where cards are common, the same shop may prefer a transfer that costs it less. The two forms stand side by side, and a reader who knows only one of them will not understand the other.
examples: The shop keeps one drawer for the smallest denomination and one for the notes.
The price is 12.50 dollars, but the money is made of dollars and cents.
In a cash economy, a market stall may not have a machine at all.
sections.heading: Coins, notes and the smallest unit

terms.example: The shop keeps one drawer for the smallest denomination and one for the notes.
terms.gloss: The value printed on a note or a coin, such as 20 or 500.

terms.example: The price is 12.50 dollars, but the money is made of dollars and cents.
terms.gloss: The smaller part of a currency, such as the cent of a dollar, that people rarely see.

terms.example: In a cash economy, a market stall may not have a machine at all.
terms.gloss: A country where most payments are still made in cash rather than by card or by transfer.

sections.body:
How you pay is a habit before it is a decision. In a produce market in Lagos, the price is spoken first and the money moves last. In a taxi in Manila, the meter is read and the driver names the fare. In a restaurant in Istanbul, the bill arrives with the food. In a supermarket in Frankfurt, the shelf carries the price and the till takes the card. All four are normal in their place. A reader who arrives with the habit of one place meets the other as an insult: the trader reads the visitor as rude, the shop reads the visitor as someone who does not know a card.

Some customs travel with the payment. The **tip** is a small sum added on top of the bill for the person who served you. In some countries it is expected, the amount is often a round share of the bill, and the price on the menu already carries a service charge; in others the service charge is on the bill and nothing more is added; in others no tip is given and nobody is offended. The sign on the door usually says which country you are in. The mistake that visitors make is to tip twice: once as a service charge and once in cash.

Two habits decide the price. The first is haggling: the first price is an opening position, and the two sides talk it down to a number both accept. The second is the fixed price: the price is the price, and the only way to change it is to find another shop. Some countries live inside one of these worlds, some cities hold both at once, and a supermarket chain keeps to the fixed price while the market next door does not. A reader learns this fast, if the reader watches where the price is spoken and where it is printed.

A bill can be shared, and the way it is shared says what the occasion is. Among colleagues the bill is split exactly, down to the last cent, and the person who pays is repaid the same day. Among older relatives, or at a family meal, one person pays and nobody counts. On a contract the split is written down, and it is the contract, not the friendship, that decides. The month has a rhythm of its own: a **payday**, the day the salary arrives and the day the shops are busiest, and then the bills, and then what is left at the end of the month. Where credit is common, the monthly bill replaces the cash: the shop does not ask for the money today, and the shopper does not have it today.

A **devaluation** is a decision by a state to lower the value of its own currency against other currencies, and it changes the price of everything a country buys. Where the state also sets the **exchange rate**, the price of the currency in another money, the market that trades outside that rate is called the **parallel market**: a street, a dealer, a bureau, a line of people with notes in their hands. Not every sum appears on the receipt. On some receipts the tax is already inside the price on the shelf, and on others it is added at the till. The card company takes its fee inside the payment. An exchange booth takes its rate inside the amount you receive, so the note you are handed holds less than the number you asked for. The receipt shows what the shop sold; it does not show who took a share on the way.
examples: The service charge is already on the bill, so there is no tip to add.
In this market the price on the stall is a starting price, and we talk about it.
The official rate has stopped working, and the parallel market sets the real price.
After the devaluation, the price of imported parts rose for everybody.
sections.heading: How money is spent: the culture of paying

terms.example: In this restaurant the service charge is on the bill, so there is no tip to add.
terms.gloss: The habit of adding a small sum on top of a bill for the person who served you.

terms.example: After the devaluation, the price of imported parts rose for everybody.
terms.gloss: A decision by a state to lower the value of its own currency against other currencies.

terms.example: Ask which day the exchange rate belongs to, because the number is only true for that day.
terms.gloss: The price of one currency expressed in the money of another currency.

terms.example: When the official rate stops working, the parallel market sets the real price of the dollar.
terms.gloss: The market that trades a currency outside the official channel, at a rate the state does not set.

sections.body:
Money carries a moral word, and the word changes with the place. In one language the word for money is close to the word for greed. In another there is a word for money that is close to the word for gift, or for luck. A reader who works across languages hears the moral charge before the number, and has to keep the two apart when writing. Flat words in a contract are not plainness for its own sake: they say the same thing to every reader.

Some cultures expect wealth to be seen. The car, the house, the clothing and the wedding are where money becomes visible, and showing it is a duty as much as a pleasure, because the wedding tells the guests whom the family can rely on. In other cultures the same money is kept out of sight: a good address is useful, but a loud car is a problem, and the saving is done quietly and without an audience. Neither of them is a lie. The difference is where the credit is kept — in what other people can see, or in what only the family knows.

Money is also a gift, and a gift of money has its own rules. In Chinese families the money for a wedding or for the new year comes in a **red envelope**, and the amount is chosen by custom rather than by a price list; certain numbers are avoided, because a number carries a meaning and some of them are unlucky. Elsewhere the gift is given plainly, in a bank account, or as a **remittance**: the money a person working abroad sends to the family at home, and often the main income of that family.

Debt is the clearest test of what a culture thinks. In some places a debt is a shame the family hides and repays in silence. In others a debt is a normal part of life, discussed openly at the table, from one neighbour to the next. The same contract, the same figures and the same monthly bill, but in one place it is a favour and in the other it is the condition of being in business. When the conversation is over, the invoice says the same thing in every country: the amount, the currency, the ISO code, the date.
examples: In this language the word for money also carries the word for greed.
The wedding is where the family shows whom it can rely on.
He sends a remittance home every month, and the rent is paid from it.
A debt is discussed openly here; it is part of being in business.
sections.heading: What money means: the culture of money

terms.example: He sends a remittance every month, and the rent is paid from it.
terms.gloss: The money a person working abroad sends to the family at home.

terms.example: The invoice ends with the ISO code and the date, in that order.
terms.gloss: The three-letter code that names a currency in the standard ISO 4217, used by banks, customs offices and computer systems.

sections.body:
A currency you do not know is not a mystery. It is a short list of facts, and you read them in a fixed order so that one never hides the next. The code first, because it removes every doubt about which money is meant. Then the symbol, then the number, then the minor unit, then the issuer, then the rate, and last the name that people use for it at home.

The order is not decoration. A symbol alone is never enough, because the same sign is used by several countries. A number alone is never enough, because the decimal mark is not the same everywhere. A rate alone is never enough, because it is true for one day and one pair of currencies. When the seven steps are done, the price in front of you is no longer a shape and a guess: it is a number, a currency, an issuer and a day.
examples: Read the code before the symbol; the symbol alone is never enough.
Check whether the currency has a minor unit before you count the coins.
Write the rate with the date and with both currencies.
sections.heading: How to read a price, a note and a currency you do not know
steps: Read the code first: find the three letters of the ISO 4217 code on the invoice, on the note or on the screen, because the code names the currency without ambiguity.
Check the symbol next: the mark on the price tells you the family of the currency, but the same mark is used by several countries, so the code settles it.
Check the separators: a comma or a dot may mark the decimals, and the two are used in opposite ways in different parts of the world, so read the price twice before you quote it.
Count the minor unit: find out how many small units make one unit of the currency, and whether the currency is divided at all, so that you do not offer coins in a country that has none.
Read the issuer: the name on the note tells you who stands behind the money and who must redeem it.
Write down the exchange rate you are given, with the date and with the two currencies, and say which one is the base currency and which one is the quote currency.
Ask for the name of the currency in the language of the country, because that is the word the people of the place use, and it is the word you need when you ask for a price.

terms.example: The first step is to read the ISO code, because it settles which money is meant.
terms.gloss: The three-letter code that names a currency in the standard ISO 4217, used by banks, customs offices and computer systems.

terms.example: Check the minor unit before you count the coins, because some currencies have none.
terms.gloss: The smaller part of a currency, such as the cent of a dollar, that people rarely see.

terms.example: Write the exchange rate with the date, because the number is only true for that day.
terms.gloss: The price of one currency expressed in the money of another currency.

terms.example: In EUR/USD the euro is the base currency and the dollar is the quote currency.
terms.gloss: The currency of the pair that the rate counts from: one unit of it is the thing you exchange.

terms.example: The rate is given in the quote currency, so a pair written EUR/USD reads in dollars.
terms.gloss: The currency of the pair that the rate is expressed in, so the rate says how many units of it you get.

sections.body:
This article explains what a currency is, it lists the currencies of 195 countries, and it explains the culture of paying and the culture of money. It does not recommend a currency, a bank, an exchange, a product or an investment. It gives no rate of exchange for today, because a rate is the number of one day and this article is not a price list.

The reason is simple. Advice about money depends on your own situation, on the prices where you live, and on rules that change from one year to the next. What this article gives you is the words: with them you can read any invoice, any board of rates and any contract, in any country.
examples: This article explains the currencies; it does not recommend a bank or an exchange.
A rate is the number of one day, so ask for a fresh one.
sections.heading: What this article does not do

terms.example: A rate of exchange is the number of one day, so ask for the rate you are given today.
terms.gloss: The price of one currency expressed in the money of another currency.

sections.body:
These are the sentences for a counter, an office and a contract. Each one names the thing that is really meant: the currency, the code, the rate, the date, the party who pays. Say the currency and not the money. Say the rate and the day it belongs to. Say who must pay and when.

Most trouble at a counter comes from one of three words: the currency, the rate and the date. When those three are exact, the sentence is short and nobody argues. Use the sentences below as they are, and change the parts that are yours.
examples: The price is 12.50 euros, so that is EUR, not dollars.
Can I pay in cash, or do you only take a card?
The exchange rate changes from one day to the next; which day is this rate for?
Write EUR/USD, and put the date next to it.
Is the tax inside this price, or is it added at the till?
We split the bill equally, and I will pay my share now.
The service charge is already on the bill, so no tip is needed.
The invoice must show the ISO code, not only the symbol.
The smallest coin here is one unit, so we round the total.
Please take the payment in local currency; I cannot change a foreign note.
I am sending the remittance today, and the transfer will arrive in the morning.
The contract states the amount in euros, and the payment is due in euros.
That is the price in the shop; the price on the street is a starting price, and we talk about it.
Which rate am I reading: the official one, or the rate the market gives?
The note is legal tender, so you can take it for the whole amount.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use about currency

terms.example: Write EUR/USD, and put the date next to it.
terms.gloss: The three-letter code that names a currency in the standard ISO 4217, used by banks, customs offices and computer systems.

terms.example: Which rate am I reading: the official one, or the rate the market gives?
terms.gloss: The price of one currency expressed in the money of another currency.

terms.example: The service charge is already on the bill, so no tip is needed.
terms.gloss: The habit of adding a small sum on top of a bill for the person who served you.

terms.example: The note is legal tender, so you can take it for the whole amount.
terms.gloss: The money the law accepts as the final payment of a debt, so that no one can refuse it as the wrong money.

terms.example: I am sending the remittance today, and the transfer will arrive in the morning.
terms.gloss: The money a person working abroad sends to the family at home.

item.summary: A currency is a promise, a code and a habit. After reading this article you can tell the name of a currency from its ISO 4217 code and its symbol, explain why one currency serves many countries, read a note and name its denomination and its minor unit, describe how a market, a taxi or a restaurant expects payment, and say what money means in the culture you work in.
item.title: The Currencies of 195 Countries: How They Are Used and What Money Means
